newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, U.S. say still far apart on new air accord.
newsitem.headline: Japan, U.S. say still far apart on new air accord.

text.p: Japan and the United States said on Wednesday they still had hurdles to clear in their aviation dispute but one U.S. industry official said he was optimistic that the two nations would close a deal in the next two months.

After three days of talks aimed at forging an interim aviation accord, negotiators from both countries said only that they would strive to meet their self-imposed deadline of September 30, despite their differences.

"The two sides are still far apart. Nonetheless, both sides agreed we should continue working towards the September target day for reaching an agreement," U.S. Assistant State Secretary Alan Larson told a news conference.
The next round of talks will take place August 27-29 in Washington. The talks will include industry and local government officials as well as government officials.
Despite the deadlock, one U.S. industry official said he was pleased with progress made.
"We are very pleased because we think we are on the threshold of an historical event," said Cyril Murphy, United Airlines' vice president for international affairs said in a telephone interview.
Murphy said a new pact would bring liberalisation instead of just a change to the current treaty, signed in 1952.
He said it was the first time that both sides had tabled position papers in the talks and that most of the U.S. airline industry was behind an interim deal.
"They see the opportunities here and they want our government to seize these opportunities," said Murphy.
U.S. and Japanese negotiators said they were still apart on the key issue of open skies -- the U.S-led policy of a free market without government restrictions for international air.
Washington has called on Japan to agree that any interim deal will eventually lead to open skies but Tokyo argues that the policy will only bring alliances dominated by U.S. carriers.

"The Japanese delegation did not accept the open skies, but rather advocated what it called a fully liberalised market. The Japanese concept at this time is far removed from our views on full liberalisation," Larson said.
